audience.programmeDescription: At the University of Amsterdam, students investigate how Dutch works, interpret Dutch literature and write for different audiences. The degree combines language research, literary study and public communication.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers beginner Dutch alongside substantial study in literature, rhetoric, media and cultural research. UvA teaches an extended Dutch-language sequence in linguistics, Dutch literary history and research.

componentNotes.y1-ned1: The first year includes a mandatory Dutch writing diagnostic. Academic tutoring continues across the three years. Neither carries credit.
componentNotes.y2-bound: These two courses prepare students for Taallab. Dynamiek van het Nederlands: theorie is also required for the selected third-year linguistics course.
componentNotes.y2-qual: Take both methods workshops after attending two of the year-two restricted-choice courses. The full-time binding study advice threshold is 48 EC from year one.
componentNotes.y2-textwork: Complete the first-year programme before entering this workshop. Students must pass the workshop before beginning the bachelor project.
componentNotes.y3-bound: The two courses form one of four permitted pairs. The other pairs focus on rhetoric, historical literature or modern literature.
componentNotes.y3-writing: The 6 EC writing workshop runs alongside the 12 EC supervised research project.
componentNotes.y3-research: Entry requires positive binding study advice, the completed first year, the specified year-two philosophy, choice, methods and research courses, plus the writing workshop and attendance in a coherent year-three pair. The research project includes a written report and presentation.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

BENLEAD311.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
BENLEAD311.text: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership examines the psychological, social and structural dynamics of organisations. Case discussions and research-based frameworks address motivation, leadership, group dynamics, organisational culture, power, conflict and change.

source.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.text: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

GOSPHIL111.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
GOSPHIL111.text: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.text: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

GOSPHIL311.name: Philosophy of Emotion
GOSPHIL311.text: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.text: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.text: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.text: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial perspectives. Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.

HCBPSYC211.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
HCBPSYC211.text: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models for group comparisons, categorical outcomes and latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports practical exercises; data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions to appropriate models, assumption checks and clear reporting.

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.text: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

MCCCOMM112.name: Dutch
MCCCOMM112.text: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.text: Style & Meaning studies stylistics: how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts and also in nonfiction. Students connect grammar, discourse and cognition with interpretation through frameworks for dialogue, narration, modality, deixis and text worlds. Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.text: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

MCCCOMM213.name: Rhetoric in Action
MCCCOMM213.text: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.text: Persuasive Communication studies persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis. Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.

MCCCOMM312.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
MCCCOMM312.text: Creative Communication Laboratory combines close reading and creative workshops with poetry, rhythm, sound, voice and performance. Students develop traditional or hybrid creative projects grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require them to explain their formal, conceptual and procedural choices.

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.text: Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change. Close examination of paintings develops visual analysis, while a term paper combines study of a painting on location with art-historical evidence.

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.text: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.text: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.text: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.text: Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.text: Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages.

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.text: World Myth & Literature compares mythic narratives across ancient and later traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes such as creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support literary analysis. A research paper, graphic explanation and creative retelling connect interpretation with narrative practice.

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok
MCCMEDI211.text: From T.V. to TikTok examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Television, film and digital forms connect storytelling and power with identity and imagined futures. Students compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, investigate disability representation, and develop futures-oriented creative projects.

Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.text: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
